lessons.title: Common Verbs for Daily Routines
lessons.body:
In Shona, everyday routines are described with common verbs that you will use daily. Start with these 20 essential verbs: kumuka (to wake up), kusimuka (to get up), kugeza (to bathe), kupfeka (to dress), kudya (to eat), kunwa (to drink), kuenda (to go), kuuya (to come), kudzoka (to return), kushanda (to work), kudzidza (to study), kurara (to sleep), kufamba (to walk), kumhanya (to run), kutaura (to speak), kunzwa (to hear), kuona (to see), kupa (to give), kutora (to take), and kuita (to do).

Each verb changes depending on the subject. For example, 'I wake up' is 'Ndinomuka', 'you wake up' is 'Unomuka', 'he/she wakes up' is 'Anomuka'. The prefix 'ndi-' means I, 'u-' means you (singular), 'a-' means he/she. For plural, 'ti-' means we, 'mu-' means you (plural), 'va-' means they. So 'we wake up' is 'Tinomuka', 'you all wake up' is 'Munomuka', 'they wake up' is 'Vanomuka'.

To talk about routine actions, use the present tense with the infix '-no-'. For example, 'Ndinodya sadza' means 'I eat sadza'. 'Unoenda kuchikoro' means 'You go to school'. 'Anoshandha mubhizimusi' means 'He works in a business'. Notice that the verb root stays the same, but the prefix changes.

Practice with real-life sentences: 'Mangwanani ndinomuka na6 am, ndinogeza, ndinopfeka, ndinodya, ndinoenda kubasa.' That means 'In the morning I wake up at 6 am, I bathe, I dress, I eat, I go to work.' At night: 'Manheru ndinodzoka kumba, ndinodya, ndinoverenga, ndinorara.' That means 'In the evening I return home, I eat, I read, I sleep.'

To make negatives, change '-no-' to '-sa-'. For example, 'Handimuke' means 'I do not wake up' (note the 'ha-' prefix for negative). But for routine, 'Handimuki mangwanani' means 'I don't wake up in the morning.' Practice these verbs by describing your own day from morning to night. Write down five sentences using different subjects. This will help you internalize the patterns.

lessons.title: Morning and Evening Routines
lessons.body:
Morning and evening routines are central to Shona daily life. In Zimbabwe, many people wake up before sunrise, especially in rural areas where farming is common. A typical morning starts with 'Mangwanani' (good morning). You might hear 'Mangwanani, wakadini?' meaning 'Good morning, how are you?' The response is 'Ndiripo' or 'Ndaswera' (I am fine).

Morning activities: 'Kumuka' (wake up), 'kusimuka' (get up), 'kugeza' (bathe), 'kupfeka' (dress), 'kudya' (eat), 'kunwa tii' (drink tea). Many families eat 'bota' (porridge) or 'sadza' with 'muriwo' (vegetables) for breakfast. If you have children, you help them prepare for school: 'Vanopfeka yunifomu' (They wear uniform). You might say 'Kurumidza, tinofamba' (Hurry, we are walking).

Evening routines: After work or school, people return home ('kudzoka kumba'). They might fetch water ('kutora mvura') or gather firewood ('kunhonga huni'). Then they cook ('kubika'). The evening meal is often eaten together. After eating, families talk ('kutaura') about the day. Children do homework ('kuita homuweki'). Then it's time to sleep ('kurara'). You say 'Urare zvakanaka' (Sleep well) or 'Rara zvakanaka'.

In urban areas, routines may differ. People might watch TV ('kuona TV') or listen to radio ('kunzwa redhiyo'). But many still follow traditional patterns. For example, in Harare, a typical evening might include 'kubika sadza' and 'kutaura nevavakidzani' (talking with neighbours).

To ask about someone's routine, use 'Unoita sei mangwanani?' (What do you do in the morning?) or 'Unoita sei manheru?' (What do you do in the evening?) Practice by describing your own routine. For example: 'Mangwanani ndinomuka na5 am. Ndinogeza, ndinopfeka, ndinodya bota, ndinoenda kubasa. Manheru ndinodzoka na6 pm, ndinobika, ndinodya, ndinoverenga bhuku, ndinorara na10 pm.' This means: 'In the morning I wake up at 5 am. I bathe, I dress, I eat porridge, I go to work. In the evening I return at 6 pm, I cook, I eat, I read a book, I sleep at 10 pm.' Try to say your routine aloud daily.

lessons.title: Talking About Work and School
lessons.body:
In Shona, talking about work and school is essential for daily conversations. Start with key vocabulary: basa (work), chikoro (school), mudzidzisi (teacher), mudzidzi (student), bhizimusi (business), mubatsiri (assistant), homuweki (homework), bvunzo (exam), kirabhu (club), nhandare (field). Common verbs: kushanda (to work), kudzidza (to learn/study), kudzidzisa (to teach), kuenda (to go), kuuya (to come), kupedza (to finish), kutanga (to start).

To say where you work, use 'Ndinoshanda ku...' (I work at...). For example: 'Ndinoshanda kuchipatara' (I work at the hospital). 'Ndinoshanda mubhizimusi' (I work in a business). To ask someone's job: 'Unoita basa rei?' (What work do you do?) or 'Unoshanda kupi?' (Where do you work?) The response: 'Ndinoshanda kuchikoro' (I work at a school). If you are a teacher: 'Ndinodzidzisa' (I teach). If you are a student: 'Ndinodzidza' (I learn).

For school, common phrases: 'Ndinodzidza kuchikoro' (I study at school). 'Mudzidzisi anodzidzisa vadzidzi' (The teacher teaches students). 'Tinodzidza Chishona' (We learn Shona). 'Ndinoverenga bhuku' (I read a book). 'Ndinonyora' (I write). 'Ndinoteerera' (I listen). 'Ndinobvunza' (I ask). 'Ndinopindura' (I answer).

To talk about your daily schedule at work or school: 'Ndinotanga basa na8 am' (I start work at 8 am). 'Ndinopedza basa na5 pm' (I finish work at 5 pm). 'Ndinodya masikati' (I eat lunch). 'Ndinombomira kuzorora' (I take a break). For school: 'Tinotanga chikoro na7 am' (We start school at 7 am). 'Tinopedza na1 pm' (We finish at 1 pm). 'Tinodya masikati' (We eat lunch). 'Tinoenda kumba' (We go home).

Practice with a partner. Ask: 'Unoshanda kupi?' 'Unoita basa rei?' 'Unodzidza chii?' 'Unodzidzisa chii?' Answer in full sentences. For example: 'Ndinoshanda kuchitoro. Ndinotengesa zvinhu.' (I work at a shop. I sell things.) 'Ndinodzidza kuyunivhesiti. Ndinodzidza zvokurapa.' (I study at university. I study medicine.) Use these patterns to talk about your own work or school.

lessons.title: Leisure Activities
lessons.body:
Leisure activities, or 'mabasa ekuzorora', are an important part of Shona daily life. After work or school, people enjoy various pastimes. Common leisure verbs: kutamba (to play/dance), kuimba (to sing), kuteerera mimhanzi (to listen to music), kuona bhaisikopo (to watch a movie), kuverenga (to read), kunyora (to write), kufamba (to walk), kumhanya (to run), kushambira (to swim), kubika (to cook), kuruka (to weave), kuveza (to carve).

Popular leisure activities in Zimbabwe include playing soccer ('kutamba nhabvu'), which is the most popular sport. You might say 'Tinotamba nhabvu' (We play soccer). Many young people play in local teams. Netball ('kutamba netibhori') is popular among girls. Board games like 'tsoro' (a traditional game similar to mancala) are played by all ages. You might say 'Tinotamba tsoro' (We play tsoro).

Music and dance are central. 'Kutamba' means both to play and to dance. Traditional dances like 'mbakumba' or 'jerusarema' are performed at ceremonies. You might say 'Vanotamba mbakumba' (They dance mbakumba). Singing ('kuimba') is common in church and social gatherings. 'Tinimba' (We sing).

Other leisure activities: 'Kuverenga bhuku' (reading a book), 'kuona firimu' (watching a film), 'kuteerera redhiyo' (listening to radio), 'kufamba mumunda' (walking in the field), 'kushambira murwizi' (swimming in the river). In urban areas, people might go to 'mabhar' (bars) or 'marestaurant' (restaurants).

To ask about leisure: 'Unoita sei kuzorora?' (What do you do to relax?) or 'Unofarira kutamba chii?' (What do you like to play?) Responses: 'Ndinofarira kutamba nhabvu' (I like to play soccer). 'Ndinofarira kuimba' (I like to sing). 'Ndinofarira kuverenga' (I like to read).

Practice by describing your leisure activities. For example: 'Mangwana ndichaenda kunotamba nhabvu nevamwe vakomana. Tinotamba kubva na3 pm kusvika 5 pm. Mushure, tinodya uye tinotaura.' (Tomorrow I will go to play soccer with other boys. We play from 3 pm to 5 pm. After, we eat and talk.) Use these phrases to talk about what you enjoy doing in your free time.

lessons.title: Frequency Adverbs
lessons.body:
Frequency adverbs in Shona help you say how often you do something. The most common are: nguva dzose (always), kazhinji (often), dzimwe nguva (sometimes), kashoma (rarely), handifi (never). These adverbs usually come after the verb or at the end of the sentence. For example: 'Ndinomuka nguva dzose' (I always wake up). 'Ndinodya sadza kazhinji' (I often eat sadza). 'Ndinofamba dzimwe nguva' (I sometimes walk). 'Ndinonwa doro kashoma' (I rarely drink beer). 'Handifi ndakanwa doro' (I never drink beer).

Other useful frequency words: mangwanani oga oga (every morning), masikati oga oga (every afternoon), manheru oga oga (every evening), vhiki rega rega (every week), mwedzi wega wega (every month), gore rega rega (every year). For example: 'Ndinomuka mangwanani oga oga' (I wake up every morning). 'Tinoenda kuchikoro vhiki rega rega' (We go to school every week).

To ask 'how often?', say 'Kangani?' or 'Nguva yakadini?' For example: 'Unoenda kuchikoro kangani?' (How often do you go to school?) The answer could be 'Nguva dzose' (Always) or 'Kazhinji' (Often). You can also use 'nguva imwe chete' (once), 'kaviri' (twice), 'katatu' (three times). For example: 'Ndinoshambira kaviri pavhiki' (I swim twice a week).

Placement: Adverbs can go at the end: 'Ndinodya sadza kazhinji.' Or after the verb: 'Ndinodya kazhinji sadza.' Both are correct. For emphasis, you can start with the adverb: 'Kazhinji ndinodya sadza.'

Practice by answering these questions: 'Unomuka nguva dzose here?' (Do you always wake up?) 'Unodya sadza kangani pavhiki?' (How often do you eat sadza per week?) 'Unoenda kubasa nguva dzose here?' (Do you always go to work?) Write down your answers using frequency adverbs. For example: 'Ndinomuka nguva dzose na6 am. Ndinodya sadza kazhinji. Ndinoshambira kashoma. Handifi ndakanwa doro.' (I always wake up at 6 am. I often eat sadza. I rarely swim. I never drink beer.) This will help you express how often you do your daily activities.

lessons.title: Forming Simple Sentences
lessons.body:
Forming simple sentences in Shona follows a clear pattern: Subject prefix + Tense marker + Verb + Object. For example, 'Ndinodya sadza' (I eat sadza). Here 'Ndi-' is the subject prefix for 'I', '-no-' is the present tense marker, '-dya' is the verb 'eat', and 'sadza' is the object. To make a sentence, start with the subject prefix, add the tense marker, then the verb, and finally the object if there is one.

Subject prefixes: ndi- (I), u- (you singular), a- (he/she), ti- (we), mu- (you plural), va- (they). Tense markers: -no- (present), -ka- (past), -cha- (future), -ri- (continuous). For example: 'Ndinodya' (I eat), 'Ndakadya' (I ate), 'Ndichadya' (I will eat), 'Ndiri kudya' (I am eating).

To make a negative sentence, use 'ha-' before the subject prefix and change the tense marker. For present: 'Handidye' (I do not eat). For past: 'Handina kudya' (I did not eat). For future: 'Handisi kudya' (I will not eat). Note that the verb ending changes to '-e' for present negative.

Objects come after the verb. For example: 'Ndinodya sadza' (I eat sadza). 'Ndinonwa mvura' (I drink water). 'Ndinoverenga bhuku' (I read a book). To say 'I eat it', you can use the object prefix: 'Ndinochidya' (I eat it, referring to sadza). But for beginners, using the full object noun is fine.

Questions are formed by adding 'here' at the end or changing intonation. For example: 'Unodya sadza here?' (Do you eat sadza?) 'Uri kuenda kuchikoro here?' (Are you going to school?) To answer yes: 'Hongu' or 'Ehe'. To answer no: 'Aiwa' or 'Kwete'.

Practice by building sentences. Start with simple ones: 'Ndinomuka' (I wake up). Add time: 'Ndinomuka na6 am.' Add object: 'Ndinodya bota.' Combine: 'Mangwanani ndinomuka na6 am, ndinodya bota, ndinoenda kubasa.' (In the morning I wake up at 6 am, I eat porridge, I go to work.) Write 10 sentences about your daily routine using different subjects and tenses. For example: 'Unoenda kuchikoro here? Hongu, ndinoenda kuchikoro.' (Do you go to school? Yes, I go to school.) This practice will make sentence formation automatic.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Everyday Activities in Shona

This reference module consolidates the everyday-activity vocabulary, verb patterns, frequency adverbs, and sentence frames you need to talk about daily routines in Shona. It is designed as a working desk reference for agribusiness professionals, field officers, traders, and extension staff who interact with Shona-speaking farmers, buyers, and community members across Zimbabwe and the wider Southern African region. Use it alongside the six core lessons: Common Verbs for Daily Routines, Morning and Evening Routines, Talking About Work and School, Leisure Activities, Frequency Adverbs, and Forming Simple Sentences.

1. Core Verb Set for Business and Fieldwork

Shona verbs are built from a root plus subject and tense markers. For everyday activity talk, the infinitive (ku- + root) is the safest starting form. The table below lists the highest-frequency verbs you will use when scheduling meetings, explaining routines, or negotiating with suppliers and farmers.

Table 1: High-frequency Shona verbs for daily and business routines
Shona (infinitive) English Business / field use example
kumukato wake up / get upNdinomuka na6 mangwanani â I get up at 6 a.m. to load produce.
kugezato wash / batheKugeza mbatya â washing work clothes before market day.
kudyato eatTinodya sadza nemuriwo â we eat sadza and greens.
kuendato goNdinoenda kumusika â I go to the market.
kuuyato comeUya kuchitoro â come to the shop / store.
kushandato workTinoshanda mubindu â we work in the garden/field.
kutengesato sellNdinotengesa chibage â I sell maize.
kutengato buyTinotenga mbeu â we buy seed.
kudzokato returnNdinodzoka kubasa na5 â I return from work at 5.
kurarato sleepTinorara na9 â we sleep at 9.
kuverengato read / countKuverenga mari â counting money.
kunyorato writeKunyora rondedzero â writing a record/ledger.

Source: Compiled from Dale, D. (1981) Duramazwi: A Basic Shona-English Dictionary, Mambo Press; and Peace Corps (1994) Shona Language Manual, Washington, DC.

2. Morning and Evening Routine Frames

Shona uses the same subject concord for both routine and immediate actions, with tense distinguishing them. The present habitual is marked by -no- (e.g., ndinomuka = I usually get up), while the present continuous uses -ri ku- (e.g., ndiri kumuka = I am getting up right now). This distinction is critical when you are confirming delivery times or shift schedules.

Table 2: Morning and evening routine sentence frames
Time of day Shona frame English meaning Business application
MorningNdinomuka na6 mangwanani.I get up at 6 in the morning.Confirming farmer availability for early collection.
MorningTinodya kudya kwemangwanani.We eat breakfast.Planning community meetings after breakfast.
MiddayNdinoenda kubasa masikati.I go to work in the afternoon.Scheduling second-shift deliveries.
EveningNdinodzoka kumba manheru.I return home in the evening.Confirming end-of-day stock counts.
EveningTinodya kudya kwemanheru.We eat supper.Closing the trading day with the team.
NightTinorara na9 usiku.We sleep at 9 at night.Setting rest periods for field staff.

Source: Adapted from Fortune, G. (1980) Shona Grammatical Constructions, University of Zimbabwe; and Mashiri, P. (2000) Shona Verb Morphology, University of Zimbabwe Publications.

3. Work and School Talk

In agribusiness contexts, work and school overlap: farmers attend field days, cooperative members receive training, and young people balance school with farm labour. Shona handles these with the same verb system, but noun class agreement matters. Basa (work, class 5) takes ri- concords in some constructions, while chikoro (school, class 7) takes chi-. In practice, the subject concord of the person doing the action is what you hear most: Ndinoshanda (I work), Anodzidza (he/she learns).

  • Ndine basa â I have work / I am busy.
  • Ndiri kubasa â I am at work.
  • Vana vanoenda kuchikoro â The children go to school.
  • Tinodzidza pamwe â We learn together (training sessions).
  • Mushandi anoshanda nesimba â The worker works hard.
  • Tinotengesa kuchitoro â We sell at the shop.

4. Leisure Activities

Leisure vocabulary is useful for relationship-building before and after negotiations. Common leisure verbs include kutamba (to play/dance), kuimba (to sing), kuona (to watch/see), kuteerera (to listen), and kufamba (to walk/travel). In rural Zimbabwe, leisure often overlaps with community activity: football at the growth point, church choir, or doro rechivanhu (traditional beer gatherings). Recognizing these activities helps you schedule meetings around real community rhythms rather than imposing external calendars.

5. Frequency Adverbs

Frequency adverbs sit before or after the verb depending on emphasis. The most common are:

  • nguva dzose / mazuva ose â always / every day
  • kazhinji â often / usually
  • dai dai / dzimwe nguva â sometimes
  • kashoma â rarely
  • handifi / hapana â never

Example: Ndinotengesa mazuva ose â I sell every day. Kazhinji tinodya masikati â We usually eat at midday. Handifi ndakanonoka â I am never late. Use these when discussing delivery reliability, payment cycles, or attendance patterns.

â  SAFETY AND CULTURAL WARNING

Do not assume that a Shona speaker who nods or says âhonguâ (yes) has agreed to a business term. In many Shona-speaking communities, indirect communication and saving face are important. Confirm all agreements in writing, and where possible use a trusted local interpreter or cooperative representative. Never record or photograph community members, farms, or traditional ceremonies without explicit permission â this can breach trust and, in some cases, Zimbabwean privacy and cultural heritage regulations. When discussing money, land, or family matters, use respectful forms and avoid direct contradictions in public.

6. Forming Simple Sentences â Quick Pattern Bank

Shona sentence order is SubjectâVerbâObject, but subject and object are marked on the verb, so pronouns are often omitted. The pattern below is the fastest way to build correct everyday sentences.

  1. Subject prefix + tense + verb root + object
  2. Ndi- (I) + -no- (habitual) + -tengesa (sell) + chibage (maize) â Ndinotengesa chibage â I sell maize.
  3. Ti- (we) + -no- + -shanda (work) + mubindu (in the garden) â Tinoshanda mubindu â We work in the garden.
  4. A- (he/she) + -no- + -dzidza (learn) + Shona â Anodzidza Shona â He/she learns Shona.
  5. Va- (they, polite) + -no- + -uya (come) + kumusika â Vanouya kumusika â They come to the market.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Use ku- infinitives when you are unsure of tense â they are always understood.
  • â Distinguish habitual -no- from continuous -ri ku- when confirming schedules.
  • â Match subject prefixes: ndi- (I), u- (you sg.), a- (he/she), ti- (we), mu- (you pl.), va- (they).
  • â Place frequency adverbs like mazuva ose and kazhinji close to the verb for clarity.
  • â Use basa for work, chikoro for school, musika for market, munda/bindu for field/garden.
  • â Confirm all agreements in writing â verbal âhonguâ may be politeness, not commitment.
  • â Ask permission before photographing people, farms, or ceremonies.
  • â Practice one routine sentence per day with a native speaker or language partner.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Peace Corps â Shona Language Manual (free PDF)
  • UDHR in Shona â Unicode/OHCHR official text
  • Ethnologue â Shona (sna) language profile
  • African Storybook â free Shona readers for practice
  • Government of Zimbabwe â official portal (language and agriculture policy context)

Module compiled for Rise Africa Skills â Shona Language, Everyday Activities. Business-first usage notes reflect agribusiness field practice in Zimbabwe and the SADC region.

quiz.q: What is the Shona verb for 'to wake up'?
quiz.explanation: Kumuka means 'to wake up', while kusimuka means 'to get up'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I eat sadza' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: The prefix 'Ndi-' means 'I', so 'Ndinodya sadza' means 'I eat sadza'.

quiz.q: What is the correct negative form of 'Ndinomuka' (I wake up)?
quiz.explanation: For present negative, use 'ha-' + subject prefix and change the verb ending to '-e', so 'Handimuke'.

quiz.q: What does 'Mangwanani' mean?
quiz.explanation: Mangwanani is a greeting used in the morning.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'I return home'?
quiz.explanation: Kudzoka means 'to return', so 'Ndinodzoka kumba' means 'I return home'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'work' (noun)?
quiz.explanation: Basa means 'work', while chikoro means 'school'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'The teacher teaches students'?
quiz.explanation: Mudzidzisi (teacher) anodzidzisa (teaches) vadzidzi (students).

quiz.q: What does 'Ndinoshanda kupi?' mean?
options: C) What work do you do?
quiz.explanation: Ndinoshanda means 'I work', and 'kupi' means 'where', so it means 'Where do I work?'

quiz.q: Which verb means 'to play' or 'to dance'?
quiz.explanation: Kutamba can mean both 'to play' and 'to dance' depending on context.

quiz.q: What is the most popular sport in Zimbabwe?
quiz.explanation: Soccer (nhabvu) is the most popular sport in Zimbabwe.

quiz.q: How do you say 'We play soccer'?
quiz.explanation: The prefix 'Ti-' means 'we', so 'Tinotamba nhabvu' means 'We play soccer'.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndinofarira kuimba' mean?
quiz.explanation: Kuimba means 'to sing', so 'Ndinofarira kuimba' means 'I like to sing'.

quiz.q: Which frequency adverb means 'always'?
quiz.explanation: Nguva dzose means 'always'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I never drink beer'?
quiz.explanation: 'Handifi' means 'never', and 'ndakanwa' is the past tense of 'kunwa' (to drink).

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'kazhinji'?
quiz.explanation: Kazhinji means 'often'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'How often do you go to school?'
quiz.explanation: 'Kangani' means 'how often', so 'Unoenda kuchikoro kangani?' is correct.

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'I swim twice a week'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kaviri' means 'twice', and 'pavhiki' means 'per week'.

quiz.q: What is the correct word order for a simple Shona sentence?
options: A) Subject prefix + Tense marker + Verb + Object
B) Verb + Subject prefix + Object + Tense marker
C) Object + Verb + Subject prefix + Tense marker
D) Tense marker + Verb + Subject prefix + Object
quiz.explanation: Shona sentences typically follow: Subject prefix + Tense marker + Verb + Object.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I will eat' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: The future tense marker '-cha-' gives 'Ndichadya' (I will eat).

quiz.q: What does 'Handina kudya' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Handina kudya' is the negative past tense, meaning 'I did not eat'.

quiz.q: How do you form a yes/no question in Shona?
options: B) Change the verb to negative
D) Use a rising intonation only
quiz.explanation: Adding 'here' at the end of a statement turns it into a yes/no question.

quiz.q: What is the response for 'Yes' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Hongu' means 'Yes', while 'Aiwa' and 'Kwete' mean 'No'.

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'We learn Shona'?
quiz.explanation: The prefix 'Ti-' means 'we', so 'Tinodzidza Chishona' means 'We learn Shona'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'homework'?
quiz.explanation: Homiweki is borrowed from English and means 'homework'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I start work at 8 am'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kutanga' means 'to start', so 'Ndinotanga basa na8 am' means 'I start work at 8 am'.

quiz.q: What does 'Mudzidzisi anodzidzisa' mean?
quiz.explanation: Mudzidzisi means 'teacher', and anodzidzisa means 'teaches'.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'every morning'?
quiz.explanation: 'Mangwanani oga oga' means 'every morning'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I rarely swim'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kashoma' means 'rarely', so 'Ndinoshambira kashoma' means 'I rarely swim'.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'kutamba tsoro'?
options: B) to play tsoro (a board game)
quiz.explanation: Tsoro is a traditional board game, so 'kutamba tsoro' means 'to play tsoro'.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly says 'I am eating'?
quiz.explanation: The continuous tense is formed with 'Ndiri' + verb, so 'Ndiri kudya' means 'I am eating'.
